questions.q: What two properties must a research hypothesis have to be usable, per this lesson?
options: Testable and falsifiable
Published and peer-reviewed
Quantitative and simulator-based
Short and memorable
questions.explain: The lesson states a hypothesis must be testable (some experiment could measure it) and falsifiable (some possible outcome could show it's wrong) -- length, publication status, and simulator-vs-hardware are unrelated to this definition.

questions.q: Why is 'quantum computers are powerful' not a usable hypothesis?
options: It only applies to one specific quantum device
It is grammatically incorrect
It is too short to be published
It names no measurement and no possible outcome that could disprove it
questions.explain: The lesson explains this statement is neither testable nor falsifiable because it names no specific measurement and no way the claim could come out false.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'error mitigation improves results' is unfalsifiable without more detail?
options: Because mitigation techniques cannot be measured at all
Because it names no specific comparison/baseline condition, so there is nothing concrete to measure against
Because 'improves' is not a real English word in this context
Because error mitigation never actually improves results
questions.explain: The lesson lists 'no stated comparison condition' as a common mistake -- without naming what the mitigated result is being compared against (no mitigation, a different technique, a different device), the claim has nothing concrete to fail against.

questions.q: Why isn't 'Can I implement Grover's algorithm in Qiskit' a hypothesis, per the lesson?
options: It is a valid engineering/learning task, but it has no comparison or prediction that could come out false in an interesting way
Because implementation tasks are never part of real research
Because Grover's algorithm cannot be implemented in Qiskit
Because it is too specific to ever be tested
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes implementation/engineering tasks (valid learning goals) from hypotheses, which need a comparison and a prediction that could actually be contradicted by the outcome.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a vague hypothesis leads to problems later in the experimental design stage?
options: Experimental design has nothing to do with how a hypothesis is written
Vague hypotheses cannot be written down in any template
Each blank in the hypothesis template (hardware, baseline, direction) is itself a design decision needed to build the experiment; leaving it vague just defers that decision to mid-experiment
Vague hypotheses always produce a null result
questions.explain: The lesson explains that naming the hardware, baseline, and direction in the hypothesis determines concrete design choices (noise model, control condition, statistical comparison) -- skipping them means discovering those decisions mid-experiment instead of before starting.
